blocks.text: 1. Stratified K-Fold
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444208204-1863524.png

K-Fold Cross Validation, the previous topic, rotates through K folds formed by pure random assignment, with no regard at all for how the classes happen to be distributed across those folds. Stratified K-Fold adds one crucial, targeted refinement to this exact procedure: every single fold is constructed specifically to preserve the original dataset's class proportions, not just the dataset as a whole across all K folds combined.

This directly extends the stratify parameter already previewed briefly in the Hold-Out Validation topic, where it forced a single train-test split to preserve class balance. Stratified K-Fold applies that exact same underlying idea, class-proportion preservation, to every one of the K folds in a full cross validation rotation, not just to one single split.
2. The Problem Plain K-Fold Can Create

blocks.alt: The Problem Plain K-Fold Can Create
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444208205-559045265.png

Plain K-Fold Cross Validation, covered in the previous topic, forms its K folds through pure random assignment, with no awareness of class labels at all during that assignment process. On a roughly balanced dataset, this works perfectly well, since random assignment naturally tends to distribute both classes fairly evenly across the folds anyway.

On a heavily imbalanced dataset, however, exactly the kind of imbalance already covered in depth in the Accuracy topic and throughout the Handling Imbalanced Data module, pure random assignment carries a real risk: one unlucky fold might, purely by chance, end up containing very few, or in an extreme case even zero, examples of the minority class. That particular round's test performance becomes wildly unreliable, computed from a test set that barely represents the minority class at all, and averaging this unreliable round together with the other K minus 1 rounds no longer produces the genuinely consistent, comparable estimate K-Fold Cross Validation is supposed to provide.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: This risk grows worse as K increases and as the minority class gets rarer, exactly the combination that makes stratification most valuable on precisely the kind of severely imbalanced problems already emphasized throughout the Handling Imbalanced Data module.

blocks.text: 3. How Stratification Fixes This
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444208206-757355250.png

Stratified K-Fold fixes this problem directly by constructing each fold deliberately, rather than through pure random assignment. Every single fold is built specifically to contain approximately the same proportion of each class as the full original dataset, rather than leaving that proportion to chance.

Concretely, on a dataset that is 90 percent negative and 10 percent positive overall, Stratified K-Fold ensures that every single one of the K folds is also, individually, approximately 90 percent negative and 10 percent positive, rather than allowing any one fold to drift toward a meaningfully different class mix purely by chance. This guarantees every evaluation round works with a test set that genuinely, fairly represents the minority class, exactly the guarantee plain random K-Fold cannot offer.
4. The Mechanism Behind Stratification

Stratified K-Fold achieves this proportional guarantee through a straightforward mechanism. First, the data is separated by class, forming one group containing every positive example and a separate group containing every negative example, exactly the kind of class-based grouping already implicit in the Confusion Matrix topic's four-category breakdown.

Each of these class-specific groups is then independently split into K roughly equal pieces, entirely on its own, and finally, one piece from each class-specific group is combined together to form each final fold. Since every fold is assembled by combining a proportional slice from every class, every fold ends up with a class mix proportionally matching the original full dataset, exactly the guarantee this topic covers throughout.

blocks.text: 5. Why This Matters Most on Imbalanced Data

blocks.alt: Why This Matters Most on Imbalanced Data
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444208206-884304604.png

It is worth connecting this directly back to the class imbalance concerns already covered in depth throughout this course, first in the Accuracy topic and in full depth throughout the Handling Imbalanced Data module. Imbalanced classification problems, fraud detection, rare disease diagnosis, defect detection, are precisely the situations where a reliable, honest evaluation of minority-class performance matters most, since the minority class is very often the actual class of practical interest.

Stratified K-Fold ensures the minority class gets meaningfully, proportionally represented in every single evaluation round, rather than risking a round where that minority class is nearly or entirely absent from the test fold. Without stratification, cross validation performed on an imbalanced dataset can produce genuinely misleading, unstable estimates, particularly for metrics like Recall or F1 Score that depend directly and heavily on how well the minority class specifically gets identified.
6. Stratified K-Fold as the Silent Default

blocks.alt: Stratified K-Fold as the Silent Default
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444208207-610659569.png

It is worth knowing directly that scikit-learn's cross_val_score function, already used throughout the worked examples in this module, actually uses Stratified K-Fold automatically by default whenever the underlying task is classification, rather than plain K-Fold, even without explicitly requesting it. This means several worked examples already covered earlier in this module may have silently benefited from stratification already, without it being called out explicitly at the time.

For regression tasks, by contrast, cross_val_score defaults to plain K-Fold instead, since there is no discrete class label available to stratify by in a continuous regression target, a distinction worth keeping in mind directly connects back to why Stratified K-Fold, as a named, dedicated technique, is specifically a classification-oriented refinement of the general K-Fold idea.
7. A Regression Variant: Stratifying by Binned Ranges

Stratification, as covered so far, is naturally defined in terms of discrete class labels, which raises a reasonable question: can something similar be applied to a continuous regression target, where there is no discrete class to stratify by at all? A practical, if less standardized, technique exists for exactly this situation: bin the continuous target into a set of discrete ranges first, for instance low, medium, and high value ranges, and then stratify the K-Fold split by those artificial bins instead of by a true class label.

This binned-stratification approach is not built into standard library defaults the way classification stratification is, since it requires a somewhat subjective, manual choice of how to define the bins in the first place. It remains a reasonable, sometimes genuinely valuable technique to apply manually on regression problems where the target's distribution is itself notably skewed or uneven, echoing the same underlying concern about representative folds that motivates ordinary Stratified K-Fold for classification.
8. A Practical Caveat: Classes Smaller Than K

blocks.alt: A Practical Caveat: Classes Smaller Than K
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444208207-100220967.png

Stratified K-Fold has one hard mathematical constraint worth knowing directly: it genuinely cannot work correctly if any class has fewer total examples than K itself. If a minority class contains, for instance, only 3 examples total, but K is set to 5, there is no way to distribute those 3 examples across 5 folds while keeping every single fold non-empty for that class; at least one or two folds would necessarily end up with zero examples of that minority class, defeating the entire purpose of stratification.

When this situation arises, the practical fix is either to reduce K to be no larger than the smallest class's total example count, ensuring every fold can genuinely receive at least one example of every class, or, where feasible, to gather additional examples of that especially rare minority class before attempting cross validation at all. This caveat is worth checking directly on any severely imbalanced dataset before committing to a specific K value.

blocks.title: tip
blocks.content: Always check the exact count of the rarest class in a dataset before choosing K for Stratified K-Fold. A common practical rule of thumb is to keep K no larger than roughly half of the smallest class's example count, leaving comfortable room in every fold.

blocks.text: 9. Extending to Multiclass Problems
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444208208-243818013.png

Stratified K-Fold, described so far mostly in binary terms, extends directly and naturally to multiclass classification problems, exactly the same multiclass setting already covered for Precision, Recall, F1 Score, and AUC throughout the Model Evaluation Classification module. Rather than preserving just one positive-versus-negative proportion, every fold instead preserves the proportion of every single class simultaneously, however many classes the problem actually has.

This means a ten-class digit recognition problem, evaluated with Stratified K-Fold, ensures every fold contains a genuinely representative mix of all ten digits, not just an overall balance across the dataset as a whole. This makes Stratified K-Fold just as valuable, and in a genuine sense even more valuable, on multiclass problems, where the risk of any one specific class being poorly represented in some particular fold grows with every additional class the problem has.
10. Worked Example

The example below directly compares plain K-Fold against Stratified K-Fold on a heavily imbalanced dataset, showing how class proportions can drift in plain K-Fold's folds but stay stable in Stratified K-Fold's.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
# A heavily imbalanced dataset: 95% negative, 5% positive
X_majority = rng.normal(loc=[0, 0], scale=2, size=(190, 2))
X_minority = rng.normal(loc=[4, 4], scale=2, size=(10, 2))
X = np.vstack([X_majority, X_minority])
y = np.array([0] * 190 + [1] * 10)

print("Overall positive class proportion:", y.mean())

# Plain K-Fold: check positive class proportion in each fold's test set
plain_kfold = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
print("\nPlain K-Fold, positive proportion per test fold:")
for fold_idx, (train_idx, test_idx) in enumerate(plain_kfold.split(X, y)):
    print(f"  Fold {fold_idx + 1}: {y[test_idx].mean():.3f}")

# Stratified K-Fold: same check
stratified_kfold = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
print("\nStratified K-Fold, positive proportion per test fold:")
for fold_idx, (train_idx, test_idx) in enumerate(stratified_kfold.split(X, y)):
    print(f"  Fold {fold_idx + 1}: {y[test_idx].mean():.3f}")

model = LogisticRegression()
plain_scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=plain_kfold)
strat_scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=stratified_kfold)
print(f"\nPlain K-Fold accuracy: mean={plain_scores.mean():.3f}, std={plain_scores.std():.3f}")
print(f"Stratified K-Fold accuracy: mean={strat_scores.mean():.3f}, std={strat_scores.std():.3f}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Plain K-Fold's per-fold positive proportions will typically vary noticeably around the overall 5 percent, sometimes swinging to 0 or 10 percent in a single unlucky fold, while Stratified K-Fold's proportions stay tightly, consistently close to 5 percent in every single fold, exactly the guarantee covered throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Stratified K-Fold constructs every fold to preserve the original dataset's class proportions, not just the dataset as a whole.
Plain K-Fold's pure random assignment can leave one unlucky fold badly under-representing a minority class.
It works by splitting each class separately into K pieces first, then combining one piece per class into each final fold.
This matters most on imbalanced problems, where the minority class is very often the actual class of practical interest.
scikit-learn's cross_val_score defaults to Stratified K-Fold automatically for classification tasks, plain K-Fold for regression.
A regression variant exists by binning the continuous target into ranges first, then stratifying by those artificial bins.
Stratified K-Fold mathematically cannot work if any class has fewer examples than K; reduce K or gather more minority-class data.
It extends naturally to multiclass problems, preserving the proportion of every class simultaneously in every fold.
Next up: Leave-One-Out, the extreme case of K-Fold where K equals the total number of examples in the dataset.
